title: <meta name="ai:context"> A Standard Convention for Serving Machine-Readable Page Context to AI Agents

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### What problem are you trying to solve?

JSON-LD / Schema.org is the most established solution. Structured data embedded in `<head>` is well-supported by crawlers and search engines. However, JSON-LD is optimized for structured facts (price, availability, SKU) and is poorly suited for open-ended narrative context such as styling rationale, sizing nuance, and compatibility notes. It also increases the initial HTML payload, compounding the performance problem it is meant to sidestep.

`llms.txt` is an emerging site-level convention where a Markdown file at the domain root provides AI agents with a navigable overview of the site. This addresses site-level discoverability but operates at too coarse a granularity for per-page or per-product context.

OpenGraph / meta `description` tags are widely parsed as a side effect, but are designed for social sharing previews and are too limited in scope for machine reasoning.

Proprietary APIs are used by some platforms to expose bespoke agent endpoints. These are not discoverable via standard crawling techniques and create significant fragmentation across the web.
None of these solutions provide a lightweight, standardized, per-page mechanism for pointing an AI agent to a dedicated machine-readable context resource without affecting the human-facing page experience.

### What solutions exist today?

JSON-LD / Schema.org is the most established solution. Structured data embedded in `<head>` is well-supported by crawlers and search engines. However, JSON-LD is optimized for structured facts (price, availability, SKU) and is poorly suited for open-ended narrative context such as styling rationale, sizing nuance, and compatibility notes. It also increases the initial HTML payload, compounding the performance problem it is meant to sidestep.

llms.txt is an emerging site-level convention where a Markdown file at the domain root provides AI agents with a navigable overview of the site. This addresses site-level discoverability but operates at too coarse a granularity for per-page or per-product context.

OpenGraph / meta description tags are widely parsed as a side effect, but are designed for social sharing previews and are too limited in scope for machine reasoning.

Proprietary APIs are used by some platforms to expose bespoke agent endpoints. These are not discoverable via standard crawling techniques and create significant fragmentation across the web.
None of these solutions provide a lightweight, standardized, per-page mechanism for pointing an AI agent to a dedicated machine-readable context resource without affecting the human-facing page experience.

### How would you solve it?

I propose the <meta name="ai:context"> tag: a simple, discoverable convention placed in the <head> of an HTML document that points AI agents to a dedicated Markdown file containing rich page context.

```html
<meta name="ai:context" content="https://www.example.com/ai-context/product-123.md">
```
The `content` attribute holds the URL of a Markdown file. Because this is a `<meta>` tag with a URL in content rather than a `<link>` tag, browsers do not fetch the resource. There is zero impact on page weight, render performance, or Core Web Vitals for human users. The fetch occurs only when an AI agent explicitly chooses to retrieve the resource, making it an opt-in action on the agent's part.

The Markdown format is intentional. LLMs natively understand Markdown, it is human-readable, requires no DOM parsing, and is well-suited to the mix of structured lists and narrative prose that constitutes useful agent context. It is also the natural format for content that JSON-LD cannot represent well: styling rationale, sizing quirks, compatibility notes, and curated product relationships.

This approach follows the precedent of `rel=canonical`, introduced in 2009 as a lightweight HTML signal that redirected machine consumers without altering the human experience and was later formalized as RFC 6596. It also mirrors the grassroots adoption pattern of `llms.txt`, which became a recognized convention rapidly due to its simplicity and low adoption friction.

### Anything else?

I chose the `name` attribute rather than `property` deliberately. The `property` attribute carries RDFa semantics inherited from the OpenGraph protocol and implies a linked data graph model that is unnecessary here. Using name keeps the proposal within the core HTML meta tag convention alongside `description`, `robots`, and `viewport`.

The ai: namespace prefix is proposed as a readable, intent-signaling convention consistent with existing namespacing patterns such as twitter:card. It is not semantically meaningful to the HTML parser.

For this convention to reach its potential, it requires recognition by foundational AI systems and crawlers, analogous to how search engines adopted `rel=canonical`. I believe WHATWG standardization is the appropriate path to achieving that recognition and encouraging consistent implementation across the web platform. I welcome discussion on naming, attribute design, and scope.
